prompt: Explain what a database index is and when adding one makes writes slower, for someone who has only used spreadsheets.
text:
## What a database index is

Imagine a spreadsheet with a million rows of customers. You want to find the row for "Maria Lopez." Without any help, you have to scan down the sheet, row by row, until you find her. That is slow.

A database index is a second, sorted list that the database keeps on the side. It holds the values from one column (say, last name) and, next to each value, a pointer to the row where that value lives. Because the list is sorted, the database can jump straight to "Lopez" the way you would in a phone book, instead of reading every page.

A spreadsheet comparison: it is like sorting a copy of the "Last name" column and keeping a note beside each name saying "this is row 48,213 in the real sheet." You look up the name in the sorted copy, then go directly to that row.

## Why reads get faster

- **Without an index:** the database checks every row. Ten times more rows means roughly ten times more work.
- **With an index:** the database narrows the search by halves, then jumps to the row. Ten times more rows adds only a few extra steps.

## When an index makes writes slower

The index is a separate copy of data, and the database must keep it in sync with the main table. So every write now has extra work.

- **Adding a row:** the database writes the row, then also inserts the new value into the right spot in each index. Inserting into the middle of a sorted list takes more effort than adding to the end.
- **Deleting a row:** the database must remove the matching entry from each index.
- **Changing a value in an indexed column:** the database must remove the old entry and insert a new one in the correct sorted position. Changing a column that has no index does not cause this.

In spreadsheet terms: imagine you kept three sorted copies of your data on other tabs. Every time you add a customer, you would have to update the main tab and all three sorted tabs. Reads on those tabs are quick, but each edit takes four times the work.

## How to think about the tradeoff

Indexes slow writes the most when:

- A table has many indexes, because each one needs updating.
- The table receives a lot of inserts, updates, or deletes, such as a log of events or a stream of sensor readings.
- The indexed columns change often.

Indexes are worth it when:

- You search, filter, or sort by that column often.
- The table is large. On a table with a few hundred rows, scanning is already fast, so an index gains little.
- You read much more often than you write.

A practical rule: add indexes for the columns your queries actually use to look things up, and avoid indexing everything "just in case." Each index speeds up some reads, costs some write time, and also takes up extra storage.
